en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
12. The Training Rule on Harsh Speech.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa was engaging in improper conduct.
The bhikkhus said this:
"Friend Channa, do not do such a thing;
this is not allowable."
Thus he speaks:
“Friends, what indeed do you think I am worthy of being told by you?
Surely it is I who ought to speak to you.”
"Our Buddha, our Dhamma!
Our Dhamma has been realized by our noble son!
Just as a great wind blowing might sweep together grass, sticks, leaves, and chaff, or just as a mountain stream might sweep together sand, moss, and water-weeds."
In just this way, you who have gone forth with various names, various clans, various births, and various families, have been raised up together as one.
Why, friends, do you think that it is I who should speak to you?
Indeed, it is I who should speak to you!
“The Buddha is ours, the Dhamma is ours;
our noble son has realized the Dhamma!
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“How can the Venerable Channa, when being spoken to by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, make himself one who is not to be spoken to?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Channa in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, Channa, that when you were being spoken to by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, you made yourself one who is not to be spoken to?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, when being spoken to in accordance with the Dhamma by the bhikkhus, make yourself one who is not to be spoken to?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

‘If a monk is by nature difficult to speak with, and when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma regarding the training rules included in the recitation, he makes himself unaddressable—’”
‘Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I say anything to you, venerable sirs, whether good or bad.
Venerable sirs, desist from speaking to me.
That bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus:
‘Venerable sir, do not make yourself unamenable to correction; let the venerable one make himself amenable to correction.
Let the venerable one speak to the bhikkhus in accordance with the Dhamma, and the bhikkhus will also speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dhamma.
For the Saṅgha of that Blessed One is thus developed: namely, by mutual correction and by mutual rehabilitation.’
And if that bhikkhu, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should persist as before, that bhikkhu is to be pressed by the bhikkhus up to three times for the relinquishing of that [position].
If, being pressed up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is good;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.”
"But a bhikkhu who is difficult to speak to" means he is difficult to speak to,
possessed of qualities that make him difficult to speak to, intolerant, and one who does not receive instruction respectfully.
"In regard to the training rules included in the recitation" means...
Regarding the training rules included in the Pātimokkha.
"By the bhikkhus" means by other bhikkhus.
"According to the Dhamma" means that which has been prescribed as a training rule by the Blessed One; this is what is called "according to the Dhamma.
When being addressed by such [a person], one makes oneself unaccountable for what is said.
“Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; nor shall I say anything to you, venerable sirs, whether good or bad. Venerable sirs, desist from speaking to me.
This refers to that monk who is by nature difficult to speak to.
"By the bhikkhus" means by other bhikkhus. Those who see or hear [of this] should say to him:
"Venerable sir, do not make yourself one who cannot be spoken to."
"Let the venerable one make himself subject to being spoken to.
Let the venerable one speak to the bhikkhus in accordance with the Dhamma, and the bhikkhus will also speak to the venerable one in accordance with the Dhamma.
For the Saṅgha of that Blessed One is thus trained: namely, by mutual speaking and by mutual exhortation."
He should be told a second time.
He should be told a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is good.
If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard [the charge], if they do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That bhikkhu should be dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed thus:
“Venerable sir, do not make yourself one who cannot be spoken to... [etc.
...by means of mutual rehabilitation.
He should be told a second time as well.
A third time it should be said.
If he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That bhikkhu is to be formally admonished.
And thus, monks, he is to be formally admonished:
A competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha: [text continues]
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This monk named so-and-so, when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, makes himself one who is not to be spoken to.
He does not relinquish that matter.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk named so-and-so, when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, makes himself one who is not to be spoken to.
He does not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha exhorts the monk named so-and-so for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of making him relinquish that matter, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the second time, I speak this matter... [as before]...
For a third time I speak this matter:
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This monk named so-and-so, when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, makes himself one who is not to be spoken to.
Thus he does not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha formally admonishes the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishment of that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishment of that matter, let him be silent;
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has formally admonished the monk so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent.
"I maintain this to be so.
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for the two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the motion (*ñatti*); by two formal proclamations, the serious offenses (*thullaccaya*) are suspended.
This is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
... [as before] ... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), one perceives it as a legitimate legal act and does not desist, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one is uncertain and does not desist, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If, regarding an illegal act, one perceives it as an illegal act and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If, regarding an illegal act, one perceives it as a legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, regarding an illegal act, one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who does not formally admonish [the person].
For one who relinquishes it,
for one who is insane,
and for an original offender.
The twelfth training rule on abusive speech is finished.
